title: Ireland
description: Public holidays in Ireland, from 1997, when today’s rules began

festivals.name: New Year’s Day
festivals.meaning: A public holiday in Ireland since 1975. Ireland’s public holidays don’t move when they fall at a weekend: instead, employers give a paid day off within a month, an extra day of leave, or an extra day’s pay.

festivals.name: St Brigid’s Day
festivals.meaning: Ireland’s newest public holiday, from 2023, for St Brigid of Kildare, one of Ireland’s patron saints, and Imbolc, the old start of spring. It’s the first Monday in February, or 1 February itself when that’s a Friday.

festivals.name: St Patrick’s Day
festivals.meaning: Ireland’s national day, for its patron saint, who died around 461. A public holiday since 1903.

festivals.name: Easter Monday
festivals.meaning: One of the first bank holidays, set by the Bank Holidays Act 1871. Good Friday isn’t a public holiday in Ireland.

festivals.name: June bank holiday
festivals.meaning: A public holiday since 1974, when it took the place of Whit Monday.

festivals.name: August bank holiday
festivals.meaning: One of the first bank holidays, set by the Bank Holidays Act 1871.

festivals.name: Christmas Day
festivals.meaning: The Christian feast of the birth of Jesus.

festivals.name: St Stephen’s Day
festivals.meaning: For St Stephen, the first Christian martyr. Also Wren Day, when wren boys go from door to door in straw costumes and masks.

festivals.name: Millennium public holiday
festivals.meaning: A one-off public holiday on the last day of 1999.

festivals.name: National Day of Mourning
festivals.meaning: A one-off public holiday, three days after the attacks in the United States on 11 September 2001.

festivals.name: Covid-19 public holiday
festivals.meaning: A one-off public holiday to recognise everyone’s efforts during the Covid-19 pandemic and to remember those who died. With St Patrick’s Day it made a four-day weekend.
